task: Escribe una carta al editor (130–160 palabras) defendiendo la importancia de un medio local de tu ciudad o pidiendo que exista uno. Usa conectores de causa y consecuencia.
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, almost every town of a reasonable size had its own newspaper. Its reporters sat through council meetings, covered local trials, interviewed the new head of the hospital and published the results of the school football match. Few of these stories made national headlines, but together they kept communities informed.

Over the past two decades, thousands of these papers have closed. In the United States alone, researchers estimate that more than a quarter of all local newspapers have disappeared since the early 2000s, leaving many areas without any regular source of local news. These places are now described as "news deserts".

The main cause is economic. Local papers traditionally depended on advertising, especially small adverts for jobs, houses and second-hand cars. When those adverts moved to free websites and social networks, the papers lost their most reliable source of income. Many were bought by large companies that cut costs by reducing staff, so that even the papers that survived often have far fewer journalists than before.

Why does this matter? Studies suggest that when a local paper closes, fewer people vote in local elections and fewer candidates stand for office. Some research has also found that local governments borrow money at higher costs, possibly because there is nobody watching how public money is spent. In addition, people who lose access to local news tend to rely more on national media, which often focus on divisive political conflicts rather than on practical local issues.

There are signs of hope. Non-profit news organisations funded by donations and foundations have been set up in many cities. Some publications ask readers to become members rather than subscribers, and a few local newsletters run by one or two journalists have attracted thousands of readers.

None of these models has yet replaced what was lost. But they share a conviction that democracy works better when someone is paid to sit through the long, boring council meeting and tell everyone else what happened.
